explanations.answer: The hand of the LORD was upon him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives for Ezra, the scribe from Babylon. "The king had granted Ezra all his requests, for the hand of the LORD his God was upon him." (Ezra 7:6) I've asked for plenty in my day. A bigger oven, a quiet afternoon, one more shelf. Nobody ever said yes to ALL of it, so this is a big deal.

explanations.answer: The queen of Persia spoke for him
explanations.explanation: Nice guess, but no queen shows up in this verse. The text gives one reason the king said yes to Ezra's requests: "…for the hand of the LORD his God was upon him." (Ezra 7:6) That's the reason the verse hands us, so that's the one I'm sticking with.

explanations.answer: The elders of Judah stood with him
explanations.explanation: No elders of Judah are named in this verse, and Ezra is coming up from Babylon here. The verse gives the reason itself: "…for the hand of the LORD his God was upon him." (Ezra 7:6) That's the answer the text hands us. I'd keep a crowd out of the story when the text doesn't put one in.

Ezra doesn't go alone. The text says he "…went up to Jerusalem with some of the Israelites, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants." (Ezra 7:7) That's a whole traveling crew. A road trip with a choir, and I bet nobody had to fight over the radio.

Right, he has company. "…he went up to Jerusalem with some of the Israelites, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants." (Ezra 7:7) That's quite a group for one trip. Singers in the group, too, so I'm guessing it was never dull.

He starts out on the first day of the first month and arrives on the first day of the fifth month. (Ezra 7:9) Count it out on your fingers and you land on four months. Four months is a long stretch, and I get tired just carrying a tray of cookies across the kitchen.

Close, but it's a longer trip than that. Ezra leaves on the first day of the first month and arrives on the first day of the fifth month. (Ezra 7:9) From the first month to the fifth month is four months, not two. That's a lot of road for a short guess.

That's a bit too long. The text says he began the trip "…on the first day of the first month…" and arrived "…on the first day of the fifth month…" (Ezra 7:9) Count from the first month to the fifth and you get four. Nine months, and he'd have needed a second pair of sandals.

Yes, he wants to practice it. "…Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel." (Ezra 7:10) Studying a recipe is great. But the real work starts when the oven gets turned on.

The text actually says the opposite. Ezra "…had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel." (Ezra 7:10) Practice is right there in the list, sitting between study and teach. So practicing the Law is part of what he set his heart on.

That's the third one. "…to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel." (Ezra 7:10) Study, practice, teach. I like that order. You can't hand out what you haven't baked yourself.

Copying for the king isn't on the list. The verse says Ezra set his heart "…to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel." (Ezra 7:10) The third one is teaching, and it's aimed at Israel. Keep an eye on that last piece of the sentence.

Guarding it isn't one of the three. The verse says Ezra set his heart "…to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel." (Ezra 7:10) So the third thing is teaching. Not standing watch, but passing it on.

The letter opens the door wider than that. King Artaxerxes of Persia writes, "I hereby decree that any volunteers among the Israelites in my kingdom, including the priests and Levites, may go up with you to Jerusalem." (Ezra 7:13) Priests and Levites are included, but they're not the only ones. Any volunteer can come along.

That's right. King Artaxerxes of Persia says, "I hereby decree that any volunteers among the Israelites in my kingdom, including the priests and Levites, may go up with you to Jerusalem." (Ezra 7:13) Notice the word "including." The priests and Levites are in the group, but so is any Israelite who volunteers.

That's the word. Ezra is sent "…to evaluate Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand." (Ezra 7:14) The Law is the measuring stick here. The letter even says it's in his hand, so he's got the right tool for the job.

Not quite. The letter says Ezra is sent "…to evaluate Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand." (Ezra 7:14) The Law is the standard, and it's in his hand. Prophets aren't mentioned in that sentence.

Ezra is a priest himself (Ezra 7:12), so I see why you grabbed that one. But the letter says he's sent "…to evaluate Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand." (Ezra 7:14) Being a priest is a fine job, but it's not the measuring tape. Think of a cookie inspector who checks every batch against his own mood. Nope, he needs the recipe card, and Ezra's got the Law right there in his hand.

explanations.answer: Animals to offer on the altar
explanations.explanation: That's what the king says to do. Ezra is to "…buy as many bulls, rams, and lambs as needed, together with their grain offerings and drink offerings, and offer them on the altar at the house of your God in Jerusalem." (Ezra 7:17) The king puts the silver and gold toward worship at God's house. That's a lot of shopping, and I hope somebody made a list.

explanations.answer: Stone and timber for the walls
explanations.explanation: Walls aren't in this verse. The king says to buy "…bulls, rams, and lambs as needed, together with their grain offerings and drink offerings, and offer them on the altar at the house of your God in Jerusalem." (Ezra 7:17) The shopping list is about offerings on the altar. No lumber yard on this trip.

Land isn't on the king's list. He tells Ezra to "…buy as many bulls, rams, and lambs as needed, together with their grain offerings and drink offerings, and offer them on the altar at the house of your God in Jerusalem." (Ezra 7:17) The money goes to offerings for the altar. Nobody's signing a deed here.

The king gives Ezra more freedom than that. The letter says, "You and your brothers may do whatever seems best with the rest of the silver and gold, according to the will of your God." (Ezra 7:18) Nothing about sending it back. Ezra and his brothers decide, and the will of God is the guide.

That's right, there's no sending it back. "You and your brothers may do whatever seems best with the rest of the silver and gold, according to the will of your God." (Ezra 7:18) The king leaves it to Ezra and his brothers to decide what seems best. I've never been handed leftovers with that much freedom.
The word in the letter is "promptly." The king says whatever Ezra requires "…must be provided promptly…" (Ezra 7:21) No waiting around, no letting it sit. Those treasurers got an order from the top.

A whole year is way too slow for this letter. The king says that whatever Ezra requires "…must be provided promptly…" (Ezra 7:21) That word doesn't leave room for a long wait. A year would be a bit like leaving the cookies in the oven until next season.

The letter doesn't mention a review. The king writes that whatever Ezra requires "…must be provided promptly…" (Ezra 7:21) Promptly is the word he picks. I think that doesn't sound much like a committee meeting.

explanations.answer: So wrath won't fall on his realm and sons
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the king gives. "Whatever is commanded by the God of heaven must be done diligently for His house. For why should wrath fall on the realm of the king and his sons?" (Ezra 7:23) He writes it plainly in his own letter. I'd say that's a king taking the God of heaven seriously.

explanations.answer: So the people will keep paying their taxes
explanations.explanation: Taxes aren't the reason in this verse. The king asks, "For why should wrath fall on the realm of the king and his sons?" (Ezra 7:23) That's the reason he puts in the letter. Money doesn't come up there.

explanations.answer: So his own name is honored in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: The king doesn't say that in the letter. After saying the God of heaven's commands must be done diligently for His house, he gives this reason: "For why should wrath fall on the realm of the king and his sons?" (Ezra 7:23) That's his stated reason. Whatever else was on his mind, the text doesn't tell us.

Yes, the letter spells it out. "…you have no authority to impose tribute, duty, or toll on any of the priests, Levites, singers, doorkeepers, temple servants, or other servants of this house of God." (Ezra 7:24) That's a long list of people Ezra has no authority to charge. Not one name on it can be hit with a toll by him.

The letter says the opposite. "…you have no authority to impose tribute, duty, or toll on any of the priests, Levites, singers, doorkeepers, temple servants, or other servants of this house of God." (Ezra 7:24) Nobody on that list can be charged. The king made that clear in writing.

That's the job. The king tells Ezra, "…according to the wisdom of your God, which you possess, are to appoint magistrates and judges to judge all the people west of the Euphrates—all who know the laws of your God." (Ezra 7:25) So Ezra picks the people who will do the judging. I'd never trust myself to pick judges. I can barely pick a cookie shape.

Counting isn't the task in this verse. The king says Ezra is to "…appoint magistrates and judges to judge all the people west of the Euphrates—all who know the laws of your God." (Ezra 7:25) These are magistrates and judges, not people with clipboards. The word you want is judge.

Guarding isn't what the verse says. The king tells Ezra to "…appoint magistrates and judges to judge all the people west of the Euphrates—all who know the laws of your God." (Ezra 7:25) I'd picture a guard with a big stick, but the verse hands out a different job. The ones he appoints are magistrates and judges, so the word is judge.

explanations.answer: The LORD the God of his fathers
explanations.explanation: That's where Ezra sends his thanks. "Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who has put into the heart of the king to so honor the house of the LORD in Jerusalem…" (Ezra 7:27) The king wrote the letter, but Ezra gives the praise to the LORD. When something good lands on my counter, I hope I say thank you to the right One too.

The counselors are in the letter, but they're not who Ezra blesses. He says, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who has put into the heart of the king to so honor the house of the LORD in Jerusalem…" (Ezra 7:27) His praise goes to the LORD. Ezra knows who deserves the credit.

explanations.answer: The governor west of the Euphrates
explanations.explanation: No governor is named in Ezra's words here. He says, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who has put into the heart of the king to so honor the house of the LORD in Jerusalem…" (Ezra 7:27) The blessing goes to the LORD, the God of Ezra's fathers. That's the one he thanks.
